title: The First Weeks Back
author: Dario Emanuele
summary: Dario Emanuele, drawing on twelve years in secondary classrooms, distils five lessons from his first full week back into a practical guide for establishing classroom culture at the start of the year. His central argument is that routines and attention standards are not set in September and forgotten but must be explicitly modelled, rehearsed and maintained across the whole term. He grounds this in Phillippa Lally's habit-formation research, which found a median of 66 days to reach automaticity, to challenge the assumption that a routine practised in Week One is learned. The piece then moves through concrete moves: purposeful circulation during independent work as a diagnostic tool, defining physical teaching zones in the room as implicit behavioural cues, returning to modelling without frustration when routines regress later in the year, and refusing to teach over noise. On that final point he draws on Peps Mccrea's work on social norms to argue that tolerating partial attention quietly lowers the standard for everyone. The article closes by trailing a follow-up on resetting expectations mid-term.
points: Emanuele cites Lally's UCL study (a median of 66 days to reach automaticity) to argue routine rehearsal must continue well beyond the first week, especially since secondary students juggle five or six teachers' expectations daily.
He recommends rehearsing a routine up to three times in the moment, then giving feedback, moving on, and deliberately revisiting it at the next opportunity.
Active circulation during independent work turns supervision into responsive teaching by surfacing misconceptions, pace, friction points and exemplary answers in real time.
Consistent teaching, checking and desk zones in the classroom act as spatial cues that signal the mode of learning without the teacher saying a word.
Following Peps Mccrea on social norms, settling for 28 out of 30 students attending sends a signal that attention is optional and leads to a gradual erosion of the norm.
quotes: We often fall into the trap of assuming that explaining and practicing a routine once or twice during Week One means it is “learned.” It isn’t. Routines, whether it’s distributing mini whiteboards, turning for a Turn and Talk, or silent transitions, require explicit instruction, live modelling, and relentless practice.

If the execution falls short of your standard, stop and rehearse it again. A good rule of thumb is to rehearse a routine up to three times in a single moment. If it’s still not quite there, give immediate feedback, move on with the lesson, and deliberately revisit the routine at the very next opportunity.

Secondary students sit through up to five or six different lessons a day, each with varying teacher expectations. Expecting them to master your specific classroom routines after 3-5 lessons is unrealistic. Routine practice isn’t a September-only task; it’s a long-term investment that requires practice well into the term.

Once students enter independent work (e.g. “Do Now” or ”You Do”), resist the urge to stay anchored to your desk. Consistent, active circulation is a non-negotiable practice throughout the entire academic year.
When you hold these physical boundaries consistently, students instinctually anticipate what mode of learning is about to happen simply by looking at where you are standing.

When a routine regresses, go straight back to modelling. Do not simply scold or demand better performance; pause the instruction, re-model the routine explicitly, and rehearse it again. Re-establishing a standard isn’t a failure or a waste of time; it is a necessary maintenance step that preserves your classroom culture.

When you allow one or two students to doodle, rest their head on the desk, or whisper while you are explaining content, you send a silent signal that full attention is optional. That non-compliance acts as a slow leak, more students will gradually adopt the lower standard, eroding the norm until you are forced to conduct a frustrating, high-energy class “reset” weeks later.
